claim: CSNK1G2 binds to RIPK3
source: Here we report that a member of casein kinase 1 family, casein kinase 1G2, CSNK1G2, binds and inhibits the activation of receptor-interacting kinase 3, RIPK3, thereby attenuating RIPK3-mediated necroptosis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that CSNK1G2 binds RIPK3, and this is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in the figures.

claim: CSNK1G2 inhibits the activation of RIPK3
source: Here we report that a member of casein kinase 1 family, casein kinase 1G2, CSNK1G2, binds and inhibits the activation of receptor-interacting kinase 3, RIPK3, thereby attenuating RIPK3-mediated necroptosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents western blotting data showing reduced RIPK3 phosphorylation when CSNK1G2 is co-expressed.

claim: CSNK1G2 attenuates RIPK3-mediated necroptosis
source: Here we report that a member of casein kinase 1 family, casein kinase 1G2, CSNK1G2, binds and inhibits the activation of receptor-interacting kinase 3, RIPK3, thereby attenuating RIPK3-mediated necroptosis.
evidence: Cell viability assays demonstrate that CSNK1G2 knockout cells show enhanced necroptosis, supporting the attenuation role.

claim: The binding of CSNK1G2 to RIPK3 is triggered by auto-phosphorylation at serine 211/threonine 215 sites in its C-terminal domain
source: The binding of CSNK1G2 to RIPK3 is triggered by auto-phosphorylation at serine 211/threonine 215 sites in its C-terminal domain.
evidence: Mass spectrometry identified these phosphorylation sites, and mutational analysis showed that S211A/T215A mutants lost the ability to bind RIPK3.

claim: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed significantly enhanced necroptosis response
source: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed significantly enhanced necroptosis response and premature aging of their testis, a phenotype that was rescued by either double knockout of the Ripk3 gene or feeding the animal with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from bone marrow-derived macrophages and testis cells showing enhanced cell death in response to necroptotic stimuli.

claim: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed premature aging of their testis
source: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed significantly enhanced necroptosis response and premature aging of their testis, a phenotype that was rescued by either double knockout of the Ripk3 gene or feeding the animal with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet.
evidence: Histological analysis and physiological measurements show increased empty seminiferous tubules, enlarged seminal vesicles, and loss of reproductive function in 12-month-old knockout mice.

claim: The premature testis aging phenotype in CSNK1G2-knockout mice was rescued by double knockout of the Ripk3 gene
source: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed significantly enhanced necroptosis response and premature aging of their testis, a phenotype that was rescued by either double knockout of the Ripk3 gene or feeding the animal with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet.
evidence: The manuscript shows that Csnk1g2/Ripk3 double knockout mice maintain youthful testis features and reproductive function at 12 months.

claim: The premature testis aging phenotype in CSNK1G2-knockout mice was rescued by feeding the animal with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet
source: CSNK1G2-knockout mice showed significantly enhanced necroptosis response and premature aging of their testis, a phenotype that was rescued by either double knockout of the Ripk3 gene or feeding the animal with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet.
evidence: Data show that CSNK1G2-knockout mice fed with RIPA-56 maintain testis morphology and reproductive function similar to wild-type mice.

claim: CSNK1G2 is co-expressed with RIPK3 in human testis
source: Moreover, CSNK1G2 is also co-expressed with RIPK3 in human testis, and the necroptosis activation marker phospho-MLKL was observed in the testis of old (>80) but not young men, indicating that the testis-aging program carried out by the RIPK3-mediated and CSNK1G2-attenuated necroptosis is evolutionarily conserved between mice and men.
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis of human testis sections shows overlapping expression patterns of CSNK1G2 and RIPK3.

claim: The necroptosis activation marker phospho-MLKL was observed in the testis of old (>80) but not young men
source: Moreover, CSNK1G2 is also co-expressed with RIPK3 in human testis, and the necroptosis activation marker phospho-MLKL was observed in the testis of old (>80) but not young men, indicating that the testis-aging program carried out by the RIPK3-mediated and CSNK1G2-attenuated necroptosis is evolutionarily conserved between mice and men.
evidence: Immunohistochemical staining shows phospho-MLKL signal in testis sections from 80-89 year old men but not in 25-30 year old men.

claim: The testis-aging program carried out by RIPK3-mediated and CSNK1G2-attenuated necroptosis is evolutionarily conserved between mice and men
source: Moreover, CSNK1G2 is also co-expressed with RIPK3 in human testis, and the necroptosis activation marker phospho-MLKL was observed in the testis of old (>80) but not young men, indicating that the testis-aging program carried out by the RIPK3-mediated and CSNK1G2-attenuated necroptosis is evolutionarily conserved between mice and men.
evidence: The observation of similar expression patterns and necroptosis markers in both mouse and human testis supports evolutionary conservation.

claim: RIPK3 is an intracellular serine/threonine kinase with a key role in necroptosis
source: RIPK3 is an intracellular serine/threonine kinase with a key role in necroptosis, a regulated form of necrotic cell death (Christofferson and Yuan, 2010; Vandenabeele et al., 2010; Wallach et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on RIPK3 and necroptosis.

claim: During necroptosis, RIPK3 is activated by RIPK1 in response to TNF-family cytokines
source: During necroptosis, in response of TNF-family of cytokines, toll-like receptors (TLRs), and Z-RNAs, RIPK3 is activated either by a related kinase RIPK1, or adaptor proteins TRIF, or ZBP1/DAI, respectively (Cho et al., 2009; Degterev et al., 2008; He et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on necroptosis signaling pathways.

claim: During necroptosis, RIPK3 is activated by TRIF in response to toll-like receptors
source: During necroptosis, in response of TNF-family of cytokines, toll-like receptors (TLRs), and Z-RNAs, RIPK3 is activated either by a related kinase RIPK1, or adaptor proteins TRIF, or ZBP1/DAI, respectively (Cho et al., 2009; Degterev et al., 2008; He et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on TLR-mediated necroptosis.

claim: During necroptosis, RIPK3 is activated by ZBP1/DAI in response to Z-RNAs

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020 on Z-RNA-induced necroptosis.

claim: Activated RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL
source: Activated RIPK3 phosphorylates the mixed lineage kinase-domain-like protein, MLKL, to trigger its oligomerization and translocation from the cytosol to membranes including plasma membrane for their disruption (Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on MLKL phosphorylation by RIPK3.

claim: Phosphorylated MLKL oligomerizes and translocates from the cytosol to membranes
source: Activated RIPK3 phosphorylates the mixed lineage kinase-domain-like protein, MLKL, to trigger its oligomerization and translocation from the cytosol to membranes including plasma membrane for their disruption (Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on MLKL function in necroptosis.

claim: Necroptosis is actively suppressed by caspase-8-mediated cleavage of RIPK1 and RIPK3
source: Necroptosis is actively suppressed by caspase-8-mediated cleavage of RIPK1 and RIPK3, whose upstream activation pathway is often shared between caspase-8 and RIPK1 kinase.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations in the manuscript to published research on caspase-8's role in suppressing necroptosis.

claim: Embryonic lethality in Caspase-8 knockout mice is rescued by double knockout of Ripk3
source: Embryonic lethality in Caspase-8 knockout mice is rescued by double knockout Ripk3 or Mlkl, and cellular necroptosis induction by TNF-α or TLRs is dramatically enhanced if caspase-8 activity is suppressed (Dannappel et al., 2014; Dillon et al., 2014; Günther et al., 2011; He et al., 2009; Kaiser et al., 2011; Newton et al., 2019; Oberst et al., 2011; Rickard et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2014).

claim: One of the important physiological functions of necroptosis is to promote the aging of testis in mice
source: One of the important physiological function of necroptosis is to promote the aging of testis in mice (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: The necroptosis activation marker phosphorylated MLKL has been observed in spermatogonium stem cells and Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules of old (>18 months) but not young mouse testis

claim: Knockout of Ripk3 blocks necroptosis from occurring in mouse testis
source: Knockout Ripk3, or Mlkl, or feeding mice with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet, blocks necroptosis from occurring in mouse testis, and allows mice to maintain the youthful morphological features and the function of male reproductive system to advanced ages, when age-matched wild-type mice had lost their reproductive function (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: Knockout of Mlkl blocks necroptosis from occurring in mouse testis
source: Knockout Ripk3, or Mlkl, or feeding mice with a RIPK1 kinase inhibitor-containing diet, blocks necroptosis from occurring in mouse testis, and allows mice to maintain the youthful morphological features and the function of male reproductive system to advanced ages, when age-matched wild-type mice had lost their reproductive function (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: Casein kinases control a variety of cellular signaling functions including the circadian clock
source: Casein kinases are a large family of intracellular serine/threonine kinases that control a variety of cellular signaling functions that include the circadian clock, Wnt receptor activation, μ opioid receptor modulation, DNA repair, and hypoxia response (Davidson et al., 2005; Elyada et al., 2011; Etchegaray et al., 2009; Goldberg et al., 2017; Pangou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on casein kinase functions.

claim: Casein kinases control Wnt receptor activation
source: Casein kinases are a large family of intracellular serine/threonine kinases that control a variety of cellular signaling functions that include the circadian clock, Wnt receptor activation, μ opioid receptor modulation, DNA repair, and hypoxia response (Davidson et al., 2005; Elyada et al., 2011; Etchegaray et al., 2009; Goldberg et al., 2017; Pangou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on casein kinase functions.

claim: Several casein kinase 1 family members including CSNK1D1, CSNK1E, and CSNK1G2 bind to and inhibit RIPK3 kinase activity
source: We found several of the casein kinase (CSNK) 1 family members, including CSNK1D1, CSNK1E, and CSNK1G2, bind to and inhibit RIPK3 kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by co-expression and western blotting experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CSNK1G2 expresses at the highest level in mouse testis
source: Interestingly, CSNK1G2 expresses at the highest level in mouse testis, whose expression pattern overlaps with that of RIPK3.
evidence: Western blotting analysis of mouse tissues shows highest CSNK1G2 expression in testis (Figure 3A).

claim: The expression pattern of CSNK1G2 overlaps with that of RIPK3 in mouse testis
source: Interestingly, CSNK1G2 expresses at the highest level in mouse testis, whose expression pattern overlaps with that of RIPK3.
evidence: Immunohistochemical analysis shows co-localization of CSNK1G2 and RIPK3 in seminiferous tubules (Figure 3B).

claim: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in mouse significantly enhanced necroptosis response
source: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in mouse or multiple cell lines including cell lines derived from spermatocyte and Sertoli cells significantly enhanced necroptosis response and the Csnk1g2 knockout mice showed premature aging of their testis.
evidence: Cell viability assays and western blotting show enhanced necroptosis markers in Csnk1g2 knockout cells and mice.

claim: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in cell lines derived from spermatocyte and Sertoli cells significantly enhanced necroptosis response
source: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in mouse or multiple cell lines including cell lines derived from spermatocyte and Sertoli cells significantly enhanced necroptosis response and the Csnk1g2 knockout mice showed premature aging of their testis.
evidence: Cell viability assays show enhanced cell death in GC-2spd and 15P-1 knockout cells (Figure 3F and G).

claim: CSNK1G2 is a major negative regulator of necroptosis
source: Our results demonstrate that CSNK1G2 is a major negative regulator of necroptosis.
evidence: Multiple experiments showing enhanced necroptosis upon CSNK1G2 knockout and suppression upon CSNK1G2 overexpression support this conclusion.

claim: CSNK1D1 suppressed serine 227 phosphorylation on RIPK3
source: Among the casein kinase family members, CSNK1D1, CSNK1G2, and CSNK1E suppressed serine 227 phosphorylation on RIPK3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows reduced phospho-S227-RIPK3 when CSNK1D1 is co-expressed.

claim: CSNK1E suppressed serine 227 phosphorylation on RIPK3
source: Among the casein kinase family members, CSNK1D1, CSNK1G2, and CSNK1E suppressed serine 227 phosphorylation on RIPK3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Western blotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows reduced phospho-S227-RIPK3 when CSNK1E is co-expressed.

claim: CSNK1G2 showed the most potent suppression of RIPK3 kinase activity among CSNK1G family members
source: In particular, CSNK1G2, but not its closest family members CSNK1G1 and CSNK1G3, showed the most potent suppression of RIPK3 kinase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Western blotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows that only CSNK1G2, not CSNK1G1 or CSNK1G3, suppresses RIPK3 phosphorylation.

claim: The kinase activity of CSNK1G2 is required for its function in suppressing RIPK3
source: Two kinase-dead mutants, CSNK1G2(K75A) and CSNK1G2(D165N), failed to suppress RIPK3 kinase activity (Figure 1A), indicating that the kinase activity of CSNK1G2 is required for its function in suppressing RIPK3.
evidence: Western blotting shows that kinase-dead mutants do not reduce RIPK3 phosphorylation, and cell viability assays show they do not rescue necroptosis sensitivity.

claim: Knockout of Csnk1g2 in MEFs significantly accelerated MEF necroptosis induced by TSZ
source: Consistent with its ability to inhibit RIPK3 activity when co-expressed in 293 T cells, knockout Csnk1g2 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, MEFs, significantly accelerated MEF necroptosis induced by the combination of TNF-α (T), a Smac mimetic (S), and a pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-fmk (Z) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Cell viability assays show reduced ATP levels in Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs treated with TSZ compared to wild-type.

claim: Reintroducing wild-type CSNK1G2 into Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs mitigated the enhanced necroptosis
source: The enhanced necroptosis was mitigated by reintroducing wild-type CSNK1G2 into the Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs, but a similar level of K75A kinase-dead mutant did not restore the necroptosis inhibition activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: Cell viability assays show that wild-type CSNK1G2 rescue restores resistance to necroptosis while kinase-dead mutant does not.

claim: MEFs with Csnk1g2 knocked out showed enhanced cell death when treated with TRAIL/S/Z
source: In addition to TSZ, MEFs with their Csnk1g2 knocked out also showed enhanced cell death when treated with death-inducing cytokine TRAIL plus a Smac mimetic and z-VAD (TRAIL/S/Z), or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) plus a Smac mimetic and z-VAD (LPS/S/Z) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Cell viability assays show reduced survival in Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs treated with TRAIL/S/Z.

claim: MEFs with Csnk1g2 knocked out showed enhanced cell death when treated with LPS/S/Z
source: In addition to TSZ, MEFs with their Csnk1g2 knocked out also showed enhanced cell death when treated with death-inducing cytokine TRAIL plus a Smac mimetic and z-VAD (TRAIL/S/Z), or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) plus a Smac mimetic and z-VAD (LPS/S/Z) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Cell viability assays show reduced survival in Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs treated with LPS/S/Z.

claim: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in MEFs resulted in higher levels of phospho-RIPK3 when treated with necroptosis inducers
source: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in MEFs resulted in higher levels of phospho-RIPK3 and phospho-MLKL (Figure 1C, lanes 5 and 6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Western blotting shows increased phospho-RIPK3 signal in Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs treated with necroptosis stimuli.

claim: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in MEFs resulted in higher levels of phospho-MLKL when treated with necroptosis inducers
source: Knocking out Csnk1g2 in MEFs resulted in higher levels of phospho-RIPK3 and phospho-MLKL (Figure 1C, lanes 5 and 6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Western blotting shows increased phospho-MLKL signal in Csnk1g2 knockout MEFs treated with necroptosis stimuli.

claim: Reintroducing wild-type CSNK1G2 significantly decreased the levels of phospho-RIPK3 when cells were treated with necroptosis inducers
source: Reintroducing wild-type, but not kinase-dead, mutant CSNK1G2, significantly decreased the levels of phospho-RIPK3 and phospho-MLKL when cells were treated with necroptosis inducers (Figure 1C, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: Western blotting shows reduced phospho-RIPK3 in rescued cells with wild-type CSNK1G2.

claim: Reintroducing wild-type CSNK1G2 significantly decreased the levels of phospho-MLKL when cells were treated with necroptosis inducers
source: Reintroducing wild-type, but not kinase-dead, mutant CSNK1G2, significantly decreased the levels of phospho-RIPK3 and phospho-MLKL when cells were treated with necroptosis inducers (Figure 1C, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: Western blotting shows reduced phospho-MLKL in rescued cells with wild-type CSNK1G2.

claim: MEFs with Csnk1g2 knocked out showed more RIPK1 kinase association with RIPK3
source: MEFs with their Csnk1g2 knocked out showed more RIPK1 kinase association with RIPK3 (Figure 1D, lanes 2 and 4), indicating that CSNK1G2 suppresses necroptosis by binding to RIPK3 and preventing its recruitment to necrosome.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show increased RIPK1-RIPK3 interaction in Csnk1g2 knockout cells.

claim: CSNK1G2 suppresses necroptosis by binding to RIPK3 and preventing its recruitment to necrosome
source: MEFs with their Csnk1g2 knocked out showed more RIPK1 kinase association with RIPK3 (Figure 1D, lanes 2 and 4), indicating that CSNK1G2 suppresses necroptosis by binding to RIPK3 and preventing its recruitment to necrosome.
evidence: Co-IP data showing increased RIPK1-RIPK3 interaction in absence of CSNK1G2 supports this mechanism.

claim: Expressing Myc-tagged human CSNK1G2 reduced RIPK1 and RIPK3 interaction in HeLa cells
source: As shown in Figure 1E, expressing a Myc-tagged human CSNK1G2 reduced RIPK1 and RIPK3 interaction as measured by a co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiment (Figure 1E, lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: Co-IP experiments show reduced RIPK1 in RIPK3 immunoprecipitates when CSNK1G2 is expressed.

claim: The kinase-dead mutant of CSNK1G2 (K75A) did not co-IP with RIPK3
source: The kinase-dead mutant of CSNK1G2 (K75A) neither co-IPed with RIPK3 nor decreased RIPK1–RIPK3 interaction (Figure 1E, lanes 5 and 6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Co-IP experiments show no CSNK1G2(K75A) in RIPK3 immunoprecipitates.

claim: The kinase-dead mutant of CSNK1G2 (K75A) did not decrease RIPK1-RIPK3 interaction
source: The kinase-dead mutant of CSNK1G2 (K75A) neither co-IPed with RIPK3 nor decreased RIPK1–RIPK3 interaction (Figure 1E, lanes 5 and 6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Co-IP experiments show RIPK1-RIPK3 interaction is maintained in presence of CSNK1G2(K75A).

claim: Wild-type CSNK1G2 blocked necroptosis caused by FKBP-binding small molecule-induced dimerization of FKBP–F36V–RIPK3 fusion protein
source: Moreover, the wild-type CSNK1G2-blocked necroptosis caused by the FKBP-binding small molecule-induced dimerization of an FKBP–F36V–RIPK3 fusion protein (Li et al., 2020; Orozco et al., 2014), while the kinase-dead CSNK1G2 (K75A) mutants did not, indicating that CSNK1G2 inhibits necroptosis by directly preventing RIPK3 activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

source: Moreover, the wild-type CSNK1G2-blocked necroptosis caused by the FKBP-binding small molecule-induced dimerization of an FKBP–F36V–RIPK3 fusion protein (Li et al., 2020; Orozco et al., 2014), while the kinase-dead CSNK1G2 (K75A) mutants did not, indicating that CSNK1G2 inhibits necroptosis by directly preventing RIPK3 activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Cell viability assays show that kinase-dead CSNK1G2 does not protect against dimerizer-induced cell death.

claim: CSNK1G2 inhibits necroptosis by directly preventing RIPK3 activation
source: Moreover, the wild-type CSNK1G2-blocked necroptosis caused by the FKBP-binding small molecule-induced dimerization of an FKBP–F36V–RIPK3 fusion protein (Li et al., 2020; Orozco et al., 2014), while the kinase-dead CSNK1G2 (K75A) mutants did not, indicating that CSNK1G2 inhibits necroptosis by directly preventing RIPK3 activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The ability of CSNK1G2 to block dimerization-induced RIPK3 activation supports this mechanism.

claim: Loss of the Csnk1g2 gene did not affect the development of the knockout mice
source: Loss of the Csnk1g2 gene did not affect the development of the knockout mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports that Csnk1g2 knockout mice develop normally, though specific developmental data are not shown.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages from Csnk1g2 knockout mice showed enhanced cell death when treated with T/S/Z

evidence: Cell viability assays show reduced ATP levels in BMDM from knockout mice treated with LPS/S/Z.

claim: Csnk1g2 knockout mice died within 18 hr after TNF-α administration
source: Notably, although the Csnk1g2 knockout mice looked normal, they died within 18 hr after TNF-α administration, much quicker than their wild-type littermates, indicating that TNF-α-induced systematic sepsis was dramatically enhanced (Figure 1G).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival curves show all Csnk1g2 knockout mice died within 18 hours of TNF-α injection.

claim: TNF-α-induced systematic sepsis was dramatically enhanced in Csnk1g2 knockout mice
source: Notably, although the Csnk1g2 knockout mice looked normal, they died within 18 hr after TNF-α administration, much quicker than their wild-type littermates, indicating that TNF-α-induced systematic sepsis was dramatically enhanced (Figure 1G).
evidence: The rapid death of knockout mice after TNF-α injection compared to wild-type indicates enhanced sepsis response.

claim: Ripk3 knockout mice were totally resistant to TNF-α-induced death
source: In contrast, Ripk3 knockout mice were totally resistant to such a treatment as previously reported (Newton et al., 2014; Figure 1G).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival curves show 100% survival of Ripk3 knockout mice after TNF-α injection, consistent with published literature.

claim: Three clusters of peptides of CSNK1G2 contained phosphorylated amino acid residues at serine 26 and serine 27

evidence: Mass spectrometry analysis identified phosphorylated peptides containing these residues.

claim: Only the S211A/T215A mutant lost the ability to block RIPK3 S227 phosphorylation
source: We subsequently introduced phosphorylation-resistant mutations in these residues and assessed their effect on RIPK3 activity. We found that only the S211A/T215A mutant lost the ability to block RIPK3 S227 phosphorylation, whereas the other two mutants containing serine 26/serine 27 and serine 381 to alanine mutations still blocked RIPK3 S227 phosphorylation as efficiently as the wild type (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
